text_a: We can no longer treat renewable energy as a distant problem that someone else will solve. The following pages argue that practical action is both possible and urgent. Consider first that solar power has become cheaper than many fossil fuel sources. The proof is clear when rooftop panels now supply a growing share of household electricity in India. Just as troubling, battery storage allows surplus energy to be saved for later use. Look at what happens when large grid batteries are now installed beside new solar plants. We should also remember that outdated electricity grids struggle to carry power from remote generation sites. Real life confirms this, since projects in rural areas sometimes wait years for a grid connection. Even more striking, government subsidies encourage households and companies to switch. The proof is clear when feed-in tariffs helped Germany expand its solar capacity quickly. Some people argue that change is too expensive, but doing nothing carries a much higher price. Every community has a role to play, from local groups to national leaders. Small decisions made by ordinary people add up to real change when they are shared widely. Excuses and delays have already cost us valuable time that we cannot recover. It is easy to feel powerless, but history shows that determined communities can shift public opinion. The way forward lies in affordable storage technology, long-term policy support and upgraded transmission networks. If we commit to these steps now, the next generation will inherit a far better situation. The choice is ours, and renewable energy will only improve if we act with determination.
text_b: When I began researching renewable energy, I was surprised by how many different angles there are. In this assignment I describe the main problems I found and some realistic ways forward. First of all, wind farms generate large amounts of electricity without direct emissions. You can see this when offshore turbines in the North Sea power millions of homes. Another thing I noticed is that green jobs offer new work to people leaving traditional energy industries. A good illustration is that installation and maintenance of turbines employ thousands of technicians. It is also worth mentioning that intermittent supply makes it difficult to match generation with demand. To give one example, solar output drops sharply in the evening when households use the most power. Then there is the fact that hydropower provides steady electricity but alters river ecosystems. You can see this when big dams have displaced communities in several countries. Before this project I had not really thought about how closely these things are connected. Talking to friends and family about it also showed me that people hold very different opinions. I think it is easy to ignore the topic because the effects often appear slowly. From what I read, the most practical steps would be upgraded transmission networks, community-owned solar projects and retraining for energy workers. I believe these ideas are achievable if people are willing to cooperate and think about the long term. Overall, my research shows that renewable energy affects everyday life more than most people realise.

text_a: Research on artificial intelligence in education usually highlights a number of linked causes and consequences. The discussion below outlines the strongest of these and evaluates possible responses. One finding that stands out is that biased algorithms can treat some groups of students unfairly. Consider how automated screening tools have sometimes favoured certain backgrounds. Related to this, unequal access to technology may widen gaps between wealthy and poor students. The case is illustrated when pupils without home internet cannot use many smart platforms. The data also suggest that AI writing assistants raise concerns about plagiarism and weaker writing skills. Practical evidence includes the fact that many universities have rewritten their academic integrity policies. A further point is that teacher training determines whether new tools are used well or wasted. Consider how schools that bought software without training often saw little benefit. Studies in this field often disagree on the exact size of each effect, which complicates comparison. Measurement challenges mean that some trends are easier to document than others. Differences between regions suggest that local conditions strongly influence outcomes. Long-term monitoring is required to confirm whether current trends will continue. Comparisons across countries reveal that similar problems can produce very different results. Based on this evidence, the most promising responses are clear rules on acceptable AI use, funding for devices in poorer schools and regular teacher training. Each option carries costs, yet the expected benefits appear to outweigh them over time. Ultimately, the evidence indicates that artificial intelligence in education cannot be understood or managed through isolated actions.
